extracted.intended_audience: factory managers, industrial engineers, manufacturers, and entrepreneurs interested in mass production/assembly-line methods
extracted.subtask_description: Practical principles and managerial rules for organizing mass-production factories, designing assembly lines, dividing labor, automating operations, and running a productive, low-red-tape industrial organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of assembly — place tools and men in sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the tools and the men in the sequence of the operation so that each component part shall travel the least possible distance while in the process of finishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange workstations and tooling in the exact order parts are processed to minimize movement of parts; example: overhead rails and gravity feeds to bring the next operation to the worker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of assembly — use carriers/work slides
rubrics_metrics.description: Use work slides or some other form of carrier so that when a workman completes his operation, he drops the part always in the same place—which place must always be the most convenient place to his hand—and if possible have gravity carry the part to the next workman for his operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardize drop-locations and use mechanical carriers so parts are always presented consistently; reduces errors and searching for parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of assembly — use sliding assembling lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Use sliding assembling lines by which the parts to be assembled are delivered at convenient distances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement moving lines (conveyors, overhead chains, gravity-fed platforms) that deliver parts to workers at ergonomic spacing; example: initial moving line experiments on flywheel magneto.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize worker movement and avoid stooping
rubrics_metrics.description: A man shall never have to take more than one step, if possibly it can be avoided, and that no man need ever stoop over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design benches, line heights (e.g., 'man-high' work), and part presentation so workers remain stationary and comfortable; examples: raising line heights to suit squads of different heights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce cognitive load — simplify each worker's task
rubrics_metrics.description: The net result of the application of these principles is the reduction of the necessity for thought on the part of the worker and the reduction of his movements to a minimum. He does as nearly as possible only one thing with only one movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Split operations until each worker performs a single simple operation, reducing training time and variability; example: pistons and rods operation split from one man to multiple stations increasing output dramatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment and optimize line speed carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Work out speeds for each assembly; a man must not be hurried in his work—he must have every second necessary but not a single unnecessary second.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct small-scale trials to find correct conveyor speeds (examples: tried 60, 18, settled on 44 inches per minute for flywheel magneto), adjust to balance human pace and throughput.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide and subdivide labor and operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide work so that each department will do only one thing; subdivide operations so each man has fewer movements and can be trained quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Departmentalize production into small units or 'little factories' each making or assembling a single part; example: motor assembly divided into eighty-four operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use unit production machinery adapted to a single part
rubrics_metrics.description: Each part which we have to cast has a unit or units of its own—the machinery of the unit is adapted to the single casting; thus the men in the unit each perform a single operation that is always the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design special units (overhead rails, platforms, machines) tailored to high-volume, single-part production to maximize repeatability and throughput.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automate every operation possible; eliminate manual handling
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no manual handling of material. There is not a single hand operation. If a machine can be made automatic, it is made automatic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace hand operations with machines or conveyors (examples: painting axle machine, radiator core machine, automatic press replacing 12 men), separate transportation department so workers never lift or truck materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design parts for ease of manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: All the parts are designed so that they can be most easily made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engineer product components with manufacturing simplicity in mind; designing for manufacturability reduces tooling, time, and specialised skill needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep work continuously in motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Dividing and subdividing operations, keeping the work in motion—those are the keynotes of production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure continuous flow on assembly lines and through departments to minimize queuing, handling, and idle time; examples: reduction in travel distance for cylinder casting from 4,000 to ~300 feet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate transportation from production labour
rubrics_metrics.description: No workman has anything to do with moving or lifting anything. That is all in a separate department—the department of transportation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create dedicated material-handling departments using mechanized trucks/chasises to move materials, freeing assemblers to focus on assembly tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentrate skilled labor in toolmaking and design, not routine production
rubrics_metrics.description: Our skilled men are the tool makers, the experimental workmen, the machinists, and the pattern makers...they should not be wasted in doing that which the machines they contrive can do better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use highly skilled workers to create tools, jigs, and machines that enable unskilled workers to perform repetitive tasks quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hire for potential and willingness to work, not past pedigree
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not hire experts—we do not hire men on past experiences or for any position other than the lowest...we do not care in the least about a man's antecedents—we do not even inquire from which place he has graduated. All that he needs is the desire to work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recruit widely (including foreigners and those with poor past histories), put hires at the bottom, and promote based on demonstrated ability; require ability to learn job within hours/days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require quick demonstrable productivity from rank-and-file hires
rubrics_metrics.description: The rank and file of men come to us unskilled; they learn their jobs within a few hours or a few days. If they do not learn within that time they will never be of any use to us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set short learning windows and productivity expectations; workers must be able to produce enough to cover their overhead on the floor space they occupy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flatten organization — avoid excessive titles and red tape
rubrics_metrics.description: That which one has to fight hardest against in bringing together a large number of people to do work is excess organization and consequent red tape...A few may be legally necessary...but for the rest the best rule is simple: 'Get rid of them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimize hierarchical layers, titles, and formal passing-of-messages; allow direct communication from any worker to any responsible manager to speed problem resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make individual responsibility complete
rubrics_metrics.description: The straw boss is responsible for the workmen under him. The foreman is responsible for his group. The department head is responsible for the department...Every man has to know what is going on in his sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign clear ownership of outcomes to each role, avoid splitting responsibility among many titled positions (anti-pattern: 'passing the buck').

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage experimentation; do not be constrained by 'best practice' records
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardly a week passes without some improvement being made somewhere in machine or process, and sometimes this is made in defiance of what is called 'the best shop practice.'...If some man, calling himself an authority, says that this or that cannot be done, then a horde of unthinking followers start the chorus: 'It can't be done.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test new ideas on small scale, reward attempts even when prior records show failures, and avoid institutionalizing failure-lists that deter trying; examples: casting directly from blast furnaces and endless chain casting despite prior objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purge 'expert' complacency; value continuous improvement mindset
rubrics_metrics.description: None of our men are 'experts.' We have most unfortunately found it necessary to get rid of a man as soon as he thinks himself an expert—because no one ever considers himself expert if he really knows his job.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor employees who continually seek improvements; remove those who rest on reputation and assert impossibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use special machines sparingly; prefer adjusted regular machines when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Only about ten per cent. of our tools are special; the others are regular machines adjusted to the particular job.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance investment in specialized tooling versus adapting general-purpose machinery to the task to control capital and space usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximize machinery per floor space to reduce overhead
rubrics_metrics.description: We put more machinery per square foot of floor space than any other factory in the world—every foot of space not used carries an overhead expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optimize factory layout to increase machine density while preserving necessary working room; avoid unused floor space as an overhead burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuously analyze operations with time-and-motion techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: The foreman analyzed the motions with a stop-watch...He found that four hours out of a nine-hour day were spent in walking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply time-and-motion study to uncover wasted movement and redesign operations (example: splitting piston-rod assembly raised output from 175 to 2600 assemblies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prototype new production methods at small scale before widescale adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: We try everything in a little way first—we will rip out anything once we discover a better way, but we have to know absolutely that the new way is going to be better than the old before we do anything drastic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilot experiments (e.g., initial moving line for flywheel magneto) to measure improvements, then iterate and scale successful methods.
